claude.sample_unit: participants with diabetes (simulated cohort; 1100 sensitivity/specificity scenarios)
models_evaluated: Validated deep learning DR grading model (Li et al. 2018), threshold-adjusted to 1100 sensitivity/specificity pairs

links.outcome: Cost-effectiveness of AI decision thresholds (sensitivity/specificity operating points) versus default most-accurate threshold
links.effect: Best cost-effective threshold (96.3%/80.4%) vs status quo (93.3%/87.7%): +US$14.8 million, +839 QALYs over 30 years; six scenarios cost-saving, seven cost-effective versus the most accurate model.
links.quote: In real-world DR screening, the most accurate AI model may not be the most cost-effective.

links.outcome: Whether accuracy metrics alone (AUC-optimal threshold) capture real-world utility
links.effect: The AUC-optimal operating point (status quo) was not the most cost-effective; higher sensitivity with lower specificity yielded greater QALYs at acceptable ICER.
links.quote: The most cost-effective AI model exhibited higher sensitivity (96.3%) and lower specificity (80.4%) than the status quo.

links.outcome: Effect of local prevalence on optimal AI operating point and predictive values
links.effect: At 4%, 8%, 12% prevalence, best cost-effective AI needed higher sensitivity as prevalence rose; PPV fell (e.g., 0.397 to 0.299 at 8%) while NPV rose; urban vs rural required different sensitivity (96.9% vs 94.7%).
links.quote: In health economic settings characterized by higher prevalence and higher WTP levels, the AI necessitated higher sensitivity (paired with lower specificity) to achieve the best cost-effectiveness.

links.outcome: Expected false positives and false negatives at population prevalence for different operating points
links.effect: Best cost-effective scenario vs status quo at 4-12% prevalence: 12,756 to 18,900 more false positives, 250 to 1,028 fewer false negatives; PPV lower, NPV higher.
links.quote: Compared to the status quo, BCES required for higher sensitivity (i.e., lower specificity), showed higher NPV but lower PPV, leading to increased FP cases and decreased FN cases, gaining an extra 662-974 QALYs with an additional 11–16 million costs in the population of Lifeline Express.

links.outcome: Optimal AI cutoff selection accounting for prevalence, willingness-to-pay/resource capacity
links.effect: Optimal sensitivity/specificity varied by prevalence and WTP; at WTP over US$5000 sensitivity should exceed specificity; lower WTP favored lower sensitivity/higher specificity.
links.quote: Specifically, in settings with WTP levels over US$ 5000, sensitivity should always be higher than specificity for cost-effective consideration.

links.outcome: Setting-specific tuning of AI operating threshold for rural vs urban and age subgroups
links.effect: Best cost-effective AI needed sensitivity 94.7% (specificity 85.6%) in rural and 96.9% (77.5%) in urban settings; younger groups required higher sensitivity.
links.quote: The best cost-effective AI needed a sensitivity of 94.7% (paired specificity 85.6%) in rural settings and a sensitivity of 96.9% (paired specificity 77.5%) in urban settings.

unlisted_practices: Health economic evaluation (cost-effectiveness/ICER) of AI models at multiple sensitivity/specificity operating points before selection
Setting minimum sensitivity/specificity performance standards based on cost-effectiveness

models_evaluated: Previously validated AI model for automatic diabetic retinopathy screening, evaluated across 1100 sensitivity/specificity threshold scenarios

links.effect: Best cost-effective sensitivity/specificity was 96.3%/80.4%, higher sensitivity/lower specificity than the 93.3%/87.7% most-accurate status quo.
links.quote: The most cost-effective AI model exhibited higher sensitivity (96.3%) and lower specificity (80.4%) than the status quo.

links.effect: Specificity was lower than prior validation/other AI models; status quo sensitivity/specificity was 93.3%/87.7%, AUC 0.933.
links.quote: It should be noted that the specificity of the AI model in this real-world dataset was lower than the reported performance in its previous validation as well as other reported AI models 40 .

unlisted_practices: Cost-effectiveness modeling of AI diagnostic operating points by willingness-to-pay and disease prevalence
Rural/urban and age subgroup cost-effectiveness analyses for AI screening

models_evaluated: Automated DR grading system (Li et al., 2018)

links.outcome: cost-effectiveness and QALYs across screening decision thresholds
links.effect: Compared to accuracy-optimized status quo (93.3% sensitivity, 87.7% specificity), the best cost-effective threshold (96.3% sensitivity, 80.4% specificity) gained 839 extra QALYs for an additional US$ 14.8 million over 30 years.
links.quote: Compared to the status quo, screening using the best cost-effective AI was projected to cost an additional US$ 14.8 million but gain 839 extra QALYs for the entire population across 30 years.
